stops.name: Chuquisaca, the republic that bears his name
stops.campa: Upper Peru, freed by Sucre, has declared itself a nation and, the assembly of 1825 decreeing that the new state shall be called after its liberator, is now Bolivia: the only country on earth named for a living man. In Chuquisaca its capital receives the godfather of its baptism with festivals; he writes for the infant republic a constitution with a lifetime president, his strangest and most confessional law, and calls Bolivia his beloved daughter. The mythology pauses here at the zenith: from this point every road leads down.

stops.name: Caracas, the last homecoming
stops.campa: Gran Colombia is cracking: Páez in revolt in Venezuela, Santander's lawyers against him in Bogotá. Bolívar comes home on 10 January 1827 to pardon Páez and be embraced by him under arches of triumph: statesmanship, or the beginning of surrender; the canon lets both stand. For six months he walks the streets of his and the republic's birth, ordering, endowing, remembering. On 5 July 1827 he sails from La Guaira for Bogotá. He will never see Caracas again; the city keeps the date like a wound.

stops.name: Bucaramanga, the diary of the waiting lion
stops.campa: While the Convention of Ocaña tears at the constitution, Santander's men against his, Bolívar waits out the crisis for seventy days in the small town of Bucaramanga, forbidden by decorum to attend. His French aide Perú de Lacroix writes down everything: the Liberator at chess and at mass, his opinions of Napoleon and of priests, his rages, his insomnia, his tenderness, María Teresa remembered, Piar justified. The Diario de Bucaramanga becomes the canon's most intimate gospel: the hero pacing a provincial patio while his republic unstitches.

stops.name: Bogotá, the night of September, 25 September 1828
stops.campa: Dictator now by the Organic Decree, Bolívar sleeps in the Palace of San Carlos. Past midnight the conspirators kill the sentries and break for his room; Manuela Sáenz, shaking him awake, arms him, delays him from dying sword in hand, and sends him out the window while she faces the blades alone and is beaten for it. Under the arch of the Carmen bridge the Liberator of half a world stands three hours in the water of the San Agustín, listening to the city hunt him. Rescued at dawn, he names her what the canon will call her forever.
stops.quote: You are the Liberatrix of the Liberator.
stops.quote_source: To Manuela Sáenz after the night of 25 September 1828 (O'Leary, Memorias; Manuela Sáenz's own accounts)

stops.name: Bogotá, resignation and the road out
stops.campa: Venezuela secedes and proscribes him by name; his body is failing; the Congreso Admirable receives his final resignation. In his last message he lays down every power and keeps only the one title. On 8 May 1830 he rides out of Bogotá toward the river and the sea with a small escort and a chest of dwindling silver, the crowds silent, some weeping, his enemies scrawling triumph on the walls. The canon closes the gate of the capital behind him like the door of a tomb: the descent of the Magdalena begins.
stops.quote: Independence is the only benefit we have acquired, at the cost of all the rest.
stops.quote_source: Message to the Congreso Admirable, Bogotá, 20 January 1830

stops.name: Cartagena, the blood of Abel
stops.campa: Down the Magdalena by boat to Turbaco and Cartagena, dying by stages, he waits for a ship to European exile that he will never board. Here the courier finds him: Sucre, the chosen one, the victor of Ayacucho, the heir, has been shot from ambush in the montaña of Berruecos on 4 June. Bolívar cries out the sentence the canon preserves as the epitaph of Gran Colombia, and those present say something in him breaks that no medicine afterward reaches: the future was Sucre, and the future has been murdered.
stops.quote: Holy God! The blood of Abel has been spilled!
stops.quote_source: On hearing of Sucre's assassination, Cartagena, 1 July 1830 (accounts of his aides; O'Leary, Memorias)

stops.name: Barranquilla, 'he who serves a revolution ploughs the sea'
stops.campa: Wintering in the river towns of Soledad and Barranquilla, propped in a chair because lying down suffocates him, the Liberator writes to General Flores of Ecuador the letter the canon reads as his political last will: twenty years of rule distilled into six conclusions of terrifying clarity: America ungovernable, revolution a furrow in the water, the only sensible thing to emigrate, the country falling inevitably into the hands of tyrants of every color and then, perhaps, back to the Europeans. Despair itself is given the dignity of doctrine.
stops.quote: America is ungovernable for us. He who serves a revolution ploughs the sea.
stops.quote_source: Letter to General Juan José Flores, Barranquilla, 9 November 1830

stops.name: Santa Marta, Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino, the last proclamation
stops.campa: On 1 December 1830 the brig Manuel lands him at Santa Marta, too weak to walk; a Spanish royalist, Joaquín de Mier, gives the dying republican his sugar estate of San Pedro Alejandrino: the canon underlines the charity of the old enemy. On 10 December, after receiving the last rites, Bolívar dictates from a red velvet armchair his final proclamation to the peoples of Colombia, forgiving, imploring union, offering his death itself as the last service. The doctors note that he rallies to dictate and sinks when it is done: the word was the last strength.
stops.quote: Colombians! You have witnessed my efforts to establish liberty where tyranny once reigned... If my death contributes to the ceasing of factions and the consolidation of the union, I shall go down in peace to my grave.
stops.quote_source: Last Proclamation of the Liberator, Hacienda de San Pedro Alejandrino, 10 December 1830

stops.name: Santa Marta, death of the Liberator, 17 December 1830
stops.campa: At three minutes past one in the afternoon of 17 December 1830, eleven years to the day since he founded Colombia at Angostura, Simón Bolívar dies in a borrowed bed and a borrowed shirt at San Pedro Alejandrino, his fortune spent on the freedom of five nations. In his final wandering he calls for the crossing: vamos, vamos; la gente no nos quiere en esta tierra; muchachos, lleven mi equipaje a bordo de la fragata. The clock in the room is stopped at the hour; the oath of Monte Sacro is discharged in full, and the canon closes over him like the sea he ploughed.
stops.quote: How shall I ever get out of this labyrinth!
stops.quote_source: Attributed last words, San Pedro Alejandrino, December 1830 (accounts of his physicians and aides; the deathbed tradition)
